messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was forty-three when it happened—a private tutoring session in the home of a wealthy family in the suburbs, a job he'd held for five years without incident. The father of the household, a man in his sixties whom Marcus had never been alone with before, had asked him to stay late to discuss his son's progress. The door closed. What began as conversation shifted into something else entirely. The man's hand on his shoulder, then his arm, the sudden physical force that made clear resistance was futile. Marcus had frozen—not from fear alone, but from a kind of dissociative shock, as though his body had become something happening to someone else. When it was over, he had driven home in silence, showered until his skin was raw, and told no one.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus returned to his tutoring schedule as though nothing had changed, but everything had. The clarity of certain moments from that afternoon haunted him—the exact pressure of the man's grip, the specific timbre of his voice, the texture of the fabric beneath his fingers. These details returned unbidden, vivid and intrusive, fragmenting his thoughts during lessons. Yet alongside these crystalline moments existed a strange fog: he could not quite articulate what had happened, could not find language adequate to the experience, and there were gaps in his memory—stretches of time he could not fully account for. The incompleteness terrified him more than the clarity. It suggested his own mind was no longer trustworthy, that his body had been violated in ways he could not even fully remember.

The violation had shattered something fundamental in Marcus's sense of himself. He came to believe that his body was no longer his own, that it had betrayed him by freezing, by not fighting hard enough, by existing in a form that could be taken. He was certain now that the world was far more dangerous than he had understood, that men—particularly men he did not know well—harbored intentions he could not predict. Most painfully, he felt profoundly alone with this knowledge, separated from the ordinary life his colleagues and acquaintances seemed to inhabit. This isolation fed a hypervigilance that became exhausting: he had to be especially careful because he could never know what might happen next.

When a student's parent reached out to shake his hand in greeting, Marcus's entire body contracted. The touch—innocent as it was—sent him back to that closed room, his threat system flaring. His vivid memories of the assault crystallized in that instant of contact, and he found himself scrutinizing the man's face for signs of predatory intent, watching for the micro-expressions that might betray hidden danger. Because he could not trust his body, because he believed he was isolated and vulnerable, he began to avoid any situation that might involve physical contact. He stopped attending faculty gatherings. He declined invitations to social events. He sat only in chairs positioned against walls or corners, where he could see the entire room and no one could approach from behind. When forced into unfamiliar spaces—a new student's home, a tutoring center he'd never visited—he would refuse the assignment, citing scheduling conflicts, his anxiety about danger in unknown environments overriding his professional obligations.

The maladaptive strategies that emerged from this hypervigilance soon calcified into routine. Marcus began smoking heavily, a way to manage the emotional intensity that threatened to overwhelm him whenever a trigger appeared. He avoided any situation that might provoke strong feeling—turning down invitations, limiting conversations to superficial topics, keeping emotional distance even from people who cared about him. His memories, now fragmented and incomplete, kept pulling him back into threat assessment. He would replay moments obsessively, searching for the missing pieces, and each replay rekindled his conviction that men posed a danger, that his body could not protect him, that he must remain vigilant and isolated. The vivid details and the gaps fed into each other, creating a loop: the clarity made the forgetting unbearable; the forgetting made him search for clarity; the searching kept the threat alive.

Now, at fifty-seven, Marcus has withdrawn almost entirely. His tutoring practice has dwindled as he has become increasingly selective about clients, refusing to work in homes where he might be alone with adult men, canceling sessions when his anxiety spikes. He smokes a pack a day. He has not been touched by another person in years. The isolation he feared has become the isolation he has constructed, brick by brick, as protection. What finally brought him to seek help was not the symptoms themselves—he had learned to live with them—but the recognition that he was disappearing, that his life had contracted to the point where he barely recognized himself. He is terrified of what talking about the assault might unleash, but he is also desperate to reclaim some version of the person he was before, to understand whether healing is even possible when your own body feels like enemy territory.
